abstract: This lecture emphasizes the critical role of developmental surveillance and screening in well-child checks to identify children at risk for delays or medical conditions. Dr. Bennett illustrates this through a case of a 10-month-old with decreased crawling and weight loss, where careful history and exam revealed truncal ataxia and a full fontanelle, leading to diagnosis of a cerebellar tumor. The talk covers the dual approach of surveillance (at every well visit) and standardized screening (at 9, 18, and 30 months for development; 18 and 24 months for autism). Key domains assessed include behavioral/emotional, language/communication, cognitive, and movement/physical development.
key_points: Developmental surveillance occurs at every well-child visit (2, 4, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 24, 30, 36 months) using milestone checklists that are not standardized or validated.
Standardized screening is recommended at 9, 18, and 30 months for general development, and at 18 and 24 months specifically for autism.
Surveillance and screening are complementary; surveillance can identify risk factors (e.g., maternal depression) while screening can detect cognitive issues not apparent on observation.
Always ask parents open-ended questions about worries or concerns regarding growth, development, or behavior, as they may reveal subtle regression.
Regression of motor skills (e.g., crawling) is a red flag that warrants thorough evaluation, including observation of the child's movement.
Truncal ataxia and a full fontanelle in an infant with motor regression point toward a cerebellar mass until proven otherwise.
Only 63% of pediatricians perform recommended developmental screening, citing lack of time and inadequate compensation, but this is a core responsibility.
Developmental milestones are assessed across four domains: behavioral/emotional, language/communication, cognitive, and movement/physical.
Risk factors identified during surveillance (e.g., maternal depression, lack of verbal interaction) should be documented in a prominent, forward-facing location in the chart.
Early diagnosis of conditions like spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is critical because gene therapy cannot reverse damage that has already occurred.
Ask parents about concerns at every visit; parental denial can delay diagnosis.
Observe the child directly for developmental red flags like not pointing or not responding to name.
